design_detail: Pooled analysis of the raw data of 10 double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover laboratory studies of MDMA in 194 healthy volunteers at the University Hospital Basel (2009-2018), asking which characteristics measured before dosing predict the acute response. Only the MDMA-alone and placebo sessions are used. The MDMA-placebo comparison was randomized within each source study, but the predictors (sex, age, CYP2D6 genotype, previous MDMA use, personality, mood just before intake) vary between people and were not randomized, so the analysis is observational. Each of 20 predictors was related to each of 25 response variables in linear mixed models with a random intercept for study, unadjusted and adjusted for dose per body weight, with standardized coefficients, semi-partial R2 and Benjamini-Hochberg correction; LASSO models ranked predictors. Missing data were multiply imputed (20 imputations). All coefficients are shown in two figures (images) and a supplementary figure; the main text reports the significant ones.
can_establish: Which characteristics measured before dosing were associated, at a given dose per body weight, with the size of MDMA's acute physiological and subjective effects in young, healthy, mostly MDMA-naive volunteers who took one oral dose of 75 or 125 mg per analysed session lying in a quiet hospital ward, and roughly how much variance each explained (semi-partial R2 of 0.05 to 0.12 for the personality and mood predictors).
cannot_establish: Whether a trait or mood causes a stronger or more anxious response (the predictors were not randomized and each was tested with dose per weight as the only covariate); anything about people with psychiatric disorders, people over 45, people with more than five previous MDMA uses, repeated doses, or settings such as parties, therapy or crowds (absent or not varied by design); or whether sex matters apart from dose per kilogram, since everyone received a fixed dose and women weighed less, so sex and dose per kilogram move together.

sample.recruitment: Paid volunteers recruited from the University of Basel campus into ten earlier crossover studies, each registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Methods › Study design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 18-45. Excluded: a history of psychiatric disorder or physical illness; lifetime illicit drug use more than 10 times (past cannabis use excepted); illicit drug use in the 2 months before or during the study; drug screens before test sessions (Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Age 25.1 (SD 4); 97 women; body weight 69 (SD 10) kg, range 46-97. 75 had used illicit substances 1-8 times: MDMA 41 (1-5 times), amphetamine or methamphetamine 18, cocaine 15, LSD 10, psilocybin 15; 79% had never used MDMA. NEO-FFI openness 33.2 (SD 6.3) against 24.5 (SD 5.5) in a normative sample, t = 19.7, p < 0.001 (Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not reported. Missing predictor and response data, mostly from the differing designs of the pooled studies, were multiply imputed; their extent is in Supplementary Table 1 (not read). One genotyping sample was missing and three participants did not consent to genotyping.
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy, screened, paid campus volunteers with little drug experience and markedly higher openness than a normative sample; the authors note that trials may attract open people. Excluding psychiatric disorders narrows the range of neuroticism and trait anxiety, and the narrow ages (SD 4 years) narrow age, both of which tend to weaken associations rather than create them.

exposure.measurement: Characteristics measured before dosing: sex; age; body weight; CYP2D6 genetic activity score; number of previous MDMA uses (self-report); mood immediately before intake on the Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS; 60 adjectives rated on 4-point scales: performance-related activity, general inactivation, extraversion, introversion, general well-being, emotional excitability, anxiety-depressiveness); personality at screening on the NEO Five Factor Inventory (60 items: neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness, conscientiousness) and the trait scale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-T, 20 items), whose timing is not stated. Dose per body weight was the covariate; MDMA plasma concentration was examined only in unadjusted models, because it is unknown at the time of dosing (Methods › Predictor variables, 1st to 6th paragraphs; Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride per analysed session, as gelatin capsules of 25 or 100 mg, 125 mg (164 people) or 75 mg (30 people), the same for women and men regardless of weight; 112 of the 164 also took 125 mg in a second session after a medication pretreatment (not analysed; the order of sessions is not given); dose per body weight 1.7 (SD 0.4) mg/kg, range 0.8-2.7; at least 7 days between sessions. Session conditions: a quiet hospital research ward with no more than two participants per session, lying in hospital beds, mostly listening to music and not physically active; the drug was given in the morning to fasting participants and a small standardized lunch was served about four hours later (Methods › Study design, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Study drug, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: No illicit drug use in the 2 months before or during the study, with drug screens before sessions; sessions combining MDMA with a pretreatment medication or another substance were excluded from this analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 months without illicit drugs by history, checked by screens before sessions; at least 7 days between drug sessions.

comparison.controls: Placebo sessions in the same people (double-blind crossover within each source study). How the placebo data enter the response variables (for example as MDMA-minus-placebo differences) is not stated in the main text. For the predictors, the comparison is between people with higher and lower values of each characteristic.
comparison.matching: None for the predictors. Each predictor was entered alone (unadjusted) or with dose per body weight (adjusted); predictors were not adjusted for one another except in the LASSO models, which used single imputation and ignored clustering by study (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectations about MDMA and reasons for taking part were not measured; setting was standardized and could not be studied (the authors say so).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (within-person placebo; the same screening applied to all sessions).

outcomes.instruments: Plasma MDMA (area under the curve 0-6 h from samples up to 6 h); peak mean arterial pressure, heart rate and tympanic temperature (readings up to 6 h); visual analogue scales for any, good and bad drug effect, high mood, drug liking and stimulated, and bidirectional scales for closeness, openness and talkative (area under the effect curve over the day); the AMRS at 1.25, 2 and 5 h; the 5D-ASC at 6 h, rating the whole session in retrospect: oceanic boundlessness, dread of ego dissolution, visionary restructuralization, plus the subscales impaired control and cognition and anxiety. All subjective measures rated by the participant (Methods › Response variables, 1st to 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments of this laboratory; the 5D-ASC subscales follow Studerus et al. (2010). Tympanic temperature is an indirect measure of core temperature.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Unpleasant or anxious reactions' are continuous self-ratings: the 5D-ASC dread of ego dissolution (called anxious ego dissolution in the Discussion), impaired control and cognition and anxiety scores, and the VAS bad drug effect; no threshold for a clinically relevant reaction is used. 'Pleasant and prosocial effects' are the VAS good drug effect, closeness and related scales and 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across all 500 tests of the adjusted models (20 predictors by 25 responses; Figure 1 legend), with the unadjusted models handled in the same way; the text reports associations that survived correction and flags uncorrected ones.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind sessions; whether participants could tell MDMA from placebo is not reported (at 125 mg it is likely; editors' note). The trait questionnaires and the outcome ratings are both self-reports, so a person's general rating style could contribute to trait-outcome associations, especially if outcomes were not placebo-corrected.

analysis.effect_sizes: Standardized coefficients (beta), Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected p and semi-partial R2. Unadjusted, plasma MDMA with: any drug effect beta = 0.48 (corrected p < 0.001, R2 0.35); mean arterial pressure 0.35 (R2 0.25); liking 0.36 (0.17); good drug effect 0.35 (0.19); stimulated 0.3 (0.44); high mood 0.29 (0.43); AMRS introversion 0.24 (0.21); 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness 0.25 (0.06); significant for 16 of 24 responses uncorrected and 8 after correction. Adjusted for dose per body weight: CYP2D6 activity with plasma MDMA beta = -0.19 (corrected p < 0.001, R2 0.1); age with heart-rate rise -0.27 (p = 0.019, R2 0.07); openness with general inactivation -0.25 (p = 0.042, R2 0.06), closeness 0.28 (p = 0.019, R2 0.08), oceanic boundlessness 0.22 (p = 0.042, R2 0.06) and visionary restructuralization 0.27 (p = 0.006, R2 0.09); neuroticism and trait anxiety with dread of ego dissolution 0.32 each (p = 0.001 and 0.004; R2 0.12 and 0.11) and with impaired control and cognition 0.26 each (p = 0.014 and 0.042; R2 0.08 and 0.07); anxiety-depressiveness and introversion just before intake with 5D-ASC anxiety 0.25 and 0.23 (p = 0.042 each; R2 0.06 and 0.05). Sex and previous MDMA use: no significant association after adjustment. LASSO: 8.6 predictors selected per response on average (5-13); dose per body weight selected for 21 of 25 responses and largest for 12.
analysis.covariates: Dose per body weight in the adjusted models; random intercept for study.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Each of the ten source studies is registered (NCT00886886, NCT00990067, NCT01136278, NCT01270672, NCT01386177, NCT01465685, NCT01771874, NCT01951508, NCT01616407, NCT03019822); the pooled predictor analysis is not described as preregistered.
analysis.selective_reporting: All adjusted and unadjusted coefficients are said to be displayed in Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1 (images, not viewable or not read here), so selective reporting of results is limited; the text describes the corrected-significant findings. The 5D-ASC was limited to its three general dimensions to reduce testing, and two subscales were added because adverse reactions were of most interest.
analysis.power: No power calculation. 194 people, but 85% received the same dose and ages were narrow, limiting the analysis of dose and age; the authors call earlier studies too small for such analyses.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In young, healthy, mostly MDMA-naive volunteers at rest in a hospital ward, the amount of MDMA in the blood was the strongest correlate of most effects, especially the pleasant and stimulant ones. Allowing for dose per kilogram, higher openness went with more closeness, oceanic boundlessness and visionary restructuralization; higher neuroticism or trait anxiety with more dread of ego dissolution and impaired control and cognition; and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before dosing with higher 5D-ASC anxiety scores; each explained 5 to 12% of the variance. Older age went with a smaller rise in heart rate and, in LASSO, more bad drug effect. Sex and previous MDMA use (five times at most) showed no significant association after adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say openness “increased the intensity of pleasant and prosocial effects of MDMA” and that neuroticism, state anxiety and an anxious or depressed mood before intake increased the likelihood of unpleasant or anxious reactions, and that the response was largely unaffected by age, sex and previous use. Gaps: (1) causal verbs for between-person associations adjusted only for dose per kilogram; (2) the anxiety predictor was trait anxiety (STAI-T), not state anxiety; (3) age predicted the heart-rate response after correction and was the most important LASSO predictor of bad drug effect, so 'largely unaffected by age' understates the age findings; (4) the explanation that women's stronger unadjusted response came from their higher dose per kilogram is an inference the fixed-dose design cannot cleanly separate from sex (dose per kilogram ranged from 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg, so the two are correlated, not inseparable); (5) the Discussion's suggestion that patients may benefit progressively over several therapy sessions as they become more open was not tested here. The abstract describes the significant findings accurately and its practical conclusion is hedged.

timeline.event: Kirkpatrick et al. pooled 220 volunteers from three laboratories and found no sex differences in acute responses; the authors cite it as in line with their sex finding.
Schmid et al., CYP2D6 genotype and MDMA response in eight pooled studies from the same laboratory, overlapping with the present sample.

Vizeli and Liechti, safety pharmacology of nine pooled studies from the same laboratory; all nine registration numbers recorded on that card appear among the ten here. The editors' card for it records higher bad-drug-effect ratings in women after allowing for dose per kilogram; this paper says it could not confirm such sex differences (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
Haijen et al., prospective naturalistic predictors of psychedelic responses, cited here for parallels with psychedelics.
Vizeli et al. applied the same approach to LSD in 213 volunteers; one source study (NCT03019822) appears in both analyses.

replication.where_it_stands: The only pooled analysis of predictors of the MDMA response found for this page. It shares its source studies with other Basel pooled analyses (Schmid et al., 2016; Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), so those papers are not independent confirmation of each other, and its LSD counterpart (Vizeli et al., 2024) shares one study and several authors. No independent laboratory has tested personality and pre-dose mood as predictors of the MDMA response, and none outside a laboratory.

funding.funder: The paper states that the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of this article. Funding of the ten source studies is not stated in this paper.
funding.declared_conflicts: M.E. Liechti is a consultant for Mind Medicine, Inc.; the other authors declare no conflicts of interest. Knowhow and data associated with this work and owned by the University Hospital Basel were licensed by Mind Medicine, Inc. after study completion; the statement says Mind Medicine had no role in financing, planning or conducting the study or the publication.
funding.affiliations_note: E. Studerus at the Division of Personality and Developmental Psychology, University of Basel; the other authors at the Division of Clinical Pharmacology and Toxicology, University Hospital Basel, which ran all ten source studies. E. Studerus and P. Vizeli contributed equally.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered prospective study across several laboratories and in clinical settings that measures openness, neuroticism, trait anxiety and mood before MDMA, includes a wider age range and more varied MDMA experience, sets dose per kilogram independently of sex, uses placebo-corrected outcomes, and tests whether these predictors improve prediction beyond dose in data not used to build the model.

domains.note: Each predictor was adjusted only for dose per body weight, with a random intercept for study; correlated predictors (neuroticism and trait anxiety, sex and weight, mood and personality) were not adjusted for one another in the inferential models. Adequate for prediction; not for the causal wording of the Conclusions.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Validated questionnaires taken before dosing (NEO-FFI personality at screening, mood immediately before intake; the timing of the STAI-T is not stated), genotype, and recorded dose and weight.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: Healthy, screened, paid campus volunteers with high openness and narrow ages; entry did not depend on the response, but the restricted ranges limit what the associations can show.
Standardized sessions; sessions with co-administered substances excluded.
Provisional: multiple imputation assuming data missing at random, mostly by design across studies; the extent is in a supplement that was not read.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-ratings in sessions where blinding probably did not hold; the main text does not say whether ratings were placebo-corrected, so trait-outcome associations could partly reflect general rating style.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: All 500 adjusted tests are displayed and false-discovery-rate corrected; not preregistered, but the reporting is complete in the figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The MDMA-placebo contrast in each source study was randomized, but this paper's question, which personal characteristics predict the response, is answered by between-person comparisons that were not randomized, so ROBINS-E is used, as on the editors' card for Schmid et al. (2016) from the same studies. Measurement is good and reporting complete; the concerns are adjustment for dose per weight only, restricted samples, uncertain placebo correction and probable unblinding. The source can be cited for associations, in healthy volunteers given MDMA in a hospital ward, of openness with more pleasant and connected effects, of neuroticism and trait anxiety with more anxious ego dissolution and impaired control, and of an anxious-depressed mood just before dosing with more acute anxiety, each modest (R2 0.05 to 0.12), and for dose per kilogram and blood level as the main correlates of the response. It should not be cited for causal effects, for people with psychiatric disorders or heavier MDMA histories, for settings outside a laboratory, or as showing that sex does not matter.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: 10 crossover studies (2009-2018), 194 healthy volunteers (97 women); one oral MDMA dose per analysed session, 125 mg (164) or 75 mg (30), made up as gelatin capsules of 25 or 100 mg, as study conditions; 112 of the 164 (seven studies of 16) took 125 mg in two sessions, alone and after a medication pretreatment, and only the MDMA-alone session was analysed (the order of sessions is not given); dose per body weight 1.7 (SD 0.4) mg/kg, range 0.8-2.7. Sessions were in a quiet hospital ward with at most two participants, lying in beds, mostly listening to music and not physically active; the drug was given in the morning after fasting, with a small lunch about four hours later.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Study drug, 1st paragraph; Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Without adjustment, MDMA plasma concentration was the strongest predictor: significant for 16 of 24 responses uncorrected and 8 after correction, most strongly any drug effect (beta = 0.48, corrected p < 0.001, semi-partial R2 0.35), then mean arterial pressure (0.35), liking (0.36), good drug effect (0.35), stimulated (0.3), high mood (0.29), AMRS introversion (0.24) and oceanic boundlessness (0.25).
key_findings.note: The semi-partial R2 values here (0.44 for stimulated, 0.43 for high mood) do not track the coefficients; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for dose per body weight: lower CYP2D6 activity predicted higher plasma MDMA (beta = -0.19, corrected p < 0.001, R2 0.1), and older age a smaller rise in heart rate (beta = -0.27, corrected p = 0.019, R2 0.07).

Adjusted for dose per body weight, higher NEO-FFI openness predicted a larger decrease in general inactivation (beta = -0.25, corrected p = 0.042, R2 0.06), more closeness (0.28, p = 0.019, R2 0.08), more oceanic boundlessness (0.22, p = 0.042, R2 0.06) and more visionary restructuralization (0.27, p = 0.006, R2 0.09).

Adjusted for dose per body weight, higher neuroticism and higher trait anxiety (STAI-T) each predicted more 5D-ASC dread of ego dissolution (beta = 0.32 each; corrected p = 0.001 and 0.004; R2 0.12 and 0.11) and more impaired control and cognition (0.26 each; p = 0.014 and 0.042; R2 0.08 and 0.07).

Mood rated on the AMRS immediately before intake: more anxiety-depressiveness and more introversion predicted higher 5D-ASC anxiety scores (beta = 0.25 and 0.23; corrected p = 0.042 each; R2 0.06 and 0.05); the 5D-ASC was completed 6 h after dosing, rating the session retrospectively.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Predictor variables, 5th paragraph; Methods › Response variables, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: LASSO: 8.6 predictors selected per response on average (range 5-13); dose per body weight was selected for 21 of 25 responses and was the most important for 12, including any drug effect, good drug effect, high mood, stimulated, liking and oceanic boundlessness, but was less important for unpleasant or anxious reactions. For bad drug effect the most important predictors were older age, then trait anxiety, then anxiety-depressiveness before intake; neuroticism was the most important for dread of ego dissolution and impaired control and cognition.

Sex was not significantly associated with any response after adjustment for dose per body weight; the authors attribute women's stronger unadjusted response to their higher dose per kilogram (fixed doses, lower body weight), and say this does not confirm earlier studies that reported sex differences after adjusting for body weight; among studies suggesting women may be more vulnerable to acute negative effects they cite Vizeli and Liechti (2017), which the Methods name as a report of safety data from these studies, while a three-laboratory study of 220 people (Kirkpatrick et al., 2014) detected no gender differences.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Methods › Study drug, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Previous MDMA use showed no association with the response; 79% had never used MDMA and the rest at most five times, so heavier use could not be assessed.
Uncorrected only (not surviving correction): older age with a smaller rise in body temperature, less liking and good drug effect, a smaller decrease in general inactivation and more bad drug effect.

Anxiety responses to MDMA were small relative to other effects; citing the same laboratory's safety analysis, the authors state that 7% of participants reported anxiety as an acute adverse effect at 125 mg.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figure, from Vizeli and Liechti (2017), not computed in this paper.

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: young, healthy, mostly MDMA-naive participants; two doses only, 85% at the higher one; the physical and social setting was standardized and could not be studied; nothing about longer-term effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions name 'state anxiety' among the predictors of unpleasant or anxious reactions, but the measure analysed was the trait scale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-T), as the Methods, Results and Discussion say.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Conclusions; Methods › Predictor variables, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the finding as trait anxiety; the state measure in this study is the AMRS anxiety-depressiveness scale.

reporting_issues.issue: In the unadjusted plasma-concentration results the semi-partial R2 values do not track the standardized coefficients: stimulated beta = 0.3 with R2 0.44 and high mood 0.29 with 0.43, against any drug effect 0.48 with 0.35. With one standardized predictor the share of variance would be near the squared coefficient (about 0.09, 0.08 and 0.23; editors' calculation); in the adjusted models R2 and squared coefficients are close.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Kenward-Roger semi-partial R2 depends on the model's degrees of freedom; these unadjusted values should not be quoted as shares of variance explained.

reporting_issues.issue: Drug-experience statements conflict: Subjects says 75 participants had used illicit substances 1-8 times under an exclusion of more than 10 lifetime uses, while Predictor variables says all had no or very limited previous experience with psychoactive substances (0-5 times). The editors' card for Vizeli and Liechti (2017), drawn from nine of the same ten studies, records an exclusion threshold of more than five lifetime occasions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph; Methods › Predictor variables, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The eligibility threshold for prior drug use in these studies cannot be stated with confidence from the Basel pooled papers; check the source trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The main text does not say how the placebo sessions entered the analysis (for example whether responses are MDMA minus placebo, or change from the pre-dose value); outcomes are described as area under the effect curve and peak values in response to MDMA.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Methods › Response variables, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: If outcomes are not placebo-corrected, associations between traits and self-ratings may partly reflect rating style rather than the drug response; the supplement may answer this.

reporting_issues.issue: One 5D-ASC dimension is called dread of ego dissolution in the Results and anxious ego dissolution in the Discussion; the mood scale is abbreviated AMRS in the Methods and ARMS in the Results; 'MDMD' appears once for MDMA.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the same scales are meant.

reporting_issues.issue: PMC marks a cited reference as retracted: Mithoefer et al. (2019), a pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy (DOI 10.1007/s00213-019-05249-5; retraction notice linked on the page as PMC11513733).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 1st and 5th paragraphs; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Cited only as background on MDMA-assisted therapy and phase 3 trials; no finding of this paper depends on it.
